tagline: Older barns and creek landscapes amid the subdivisions east of Columbus
intro: The Jefferson Township Scenic Byway passes older barns and houses, streams, slopes and stands of trees within the Columbus metropolitan area. Ohio’s Department of Transportation presents these roads as a rural and natural setting amid subdivisions. ODOT granted the township Ohio Scenic Byway status in 2003.

The township actively manages and protects the corridor’s historic character. Many of the older barns and homes date from the early 1800s. Gahanna and Columbus have annexed most of the township’s western and southern portions, leaving small township islands within the cities.

Gahanna borders the township on the west, offering a starting point beside Big Walnut Creek. East of Gahanna, the township’s landscape includes stream corridors, hills and ravines associated with Rocky Fork, Blacklick and Swisher creeks. Rocky Fork tributaries also cross New Albany, the township’s northwestern neighbor.

moments.title: Gahanna
moments.text: Two villages once faced each other across Granville Street beside Big Walnut Creek. John Clark founded Gahanna in 1849 on land his father had bought in 1814. Jesse Baughman founded neighboring Bridgeport four years later. The rivals eventually merged, keeping Gahanna’s name because Ohio already had another Bridgeport. In 1881, residents petitioned for incorporation, and the joined village held its first mayoral election that year. The creek remains central to the city’s geography, joined by Rocky Fork Creek and Sycamore Run. A creekside redevelopment and park extension begun in 2004 added public spaces, residences and places of business to Olde Gahanna.

moments.title: Blacklick
moments.text: Blacklick’s name came from its creek after its first name proved unavailable. William A. Smith established the community in 1852 as Smithville. Historian W. Edson Richmond thought the creek had been named for landowner H. G. Black, but John F. Mansfield’s 1806 Ohio map already labels it Blacklick Creek; Black was born in 1817. The stream flows through the community in southern Jefferson Township, which is also home to the township’s active Jefferson Cemetery. Its post office once stood within the community, but moved just south of it on Reynoldsburg-New Albany Road.

moments.title: New Albany
moments.text: Rocky Fork begins in the New Albany area, where Rose Run and Sugar Run cross the city from northeast to southwest. Nobel Landon and William Yantis founded the town in 1837, dividing land into lots 50 feet wide and 100 feet long. The 1980 census counted only 414 residents. Rapid growth began in the 1990s, partly through Les Wexner’s investment; changes to State Route 161 and its I-270 connection brought freeway access. Three roads divide the city center: Dublin-Granville, Johnstown Road and New Albany-Reynoldsburg Road. Blacklick Creek crosses the city’s eastern end.
